name: Lancaran
desc: The shortest non-wayang gendhing form: a 16-beat cycle closed by gong ageng, with kenong on every fourth beat, kempul interpunctions (a wela rest in the first slot) and kethuk on the off-beats.

name: Ketawang
desc: A calm, introspective 16-beat form (pTpW pTpN pTpP pTpG) with two kenong nongan per gongan, a single kempul, kethuk and the doubling kempyang between beats.

name: Ladrang
desc: A 32-beat form with four kenong nongan per gongan and three kempul (a wela rest replacing the first), twice as broad as ketawang with kempyang doubling each beat.

name: Gangsaran
desc: A driving lancaran variant on a single repeated tone, often used for battle scenes in wayang; here a compact 8-beat gong cycle with kenong and a kempul punctuation.

name: Bubaran
desc: A closing or processional piece that shares the lancaran colotomic skeleton, played to send off an audience at the end of a performance.

name: Srepegan
desc: A fast wayang form for action scenes: kenong sounds on every off-beat against kethuk on the beats, with kempul reinforcing alternate kenong and gong closing the cycle.

name: Sampak
desc: The fastest and most agitated wayang form for fight and chase scenes, with kenong striking on every beat and kempul filling between, closed by gong.

name: Ayak-ayakan
desc: A flowing wayang form accompanying puppet entrances and pathet transitions, with kenong on every fourth pulse, kethuk on the beats and a sparser kempul line.

name: Gendhing Kethuk 2 Kerep
desc: A large-form merong with the kethuk struck twice 'close together' (kerep) per kenongan, four kenong per gongan over 32 beats, sparse kempul and a closing gong ageng.

name: Gendhing Kethuk 4 Arang
desc: An expansive merong with the kethuk spaced widely (arang) once per long span, four kenongan per gongan, very sparse kempul and the great gong ageng marking the cycle end.

name: Kendhang Kalih Lancaran
desc: The two-drum (kendhang ageng plus ketipung) accompaniment for brisk lancaran: deep dhah strokes lead each gatra cadence while lighter tak/thung strokes fill the off-beats.

name: Kendhang Satunggal Ladrang
desc: The single large-drum kendhangan for solemn ladrang, with weighty dhah strokes aligning to kenong cadences and tak accents anticipating the beats.

name: Kendhang Ciblon
desc: The lively medium ciblon drum's playful slapping idiom for dance and lively passages, weaving dense dhah/tak/dung/thung interplay across the gatra.

name: Kendhang Wayangan Srepeg
desc: The medium wayangan drum driving a fast srepeg, with continuous interlocked strokes urging the action and cueing tempo changes for the puppeteer.

name: Gong Kebyar Kebyar
desc: The explosive North-Bali style (from 1914): the great gong ageng anchors the cycle with kempur and gong wadon/lanang punctuation under blazing unison reyong and gangsa figuration.

name: Kotekan Polos
desc: The 'simple' on-beat half of a Balinese interlocking kotekan figuration, mostly falling on the beat while the sangsih answers off it; gong closes the cycle.

name: Kotekan Sangsih
desc: The 'differing' off-beat half of the interlocking kotekan that dovetails with polos to produce a single rapid composite melody in gong kebyar.

name: Kotekan Telu
desc: A three-note interlocking kotekan figuration whose polos and sangsih each strike groups of three, combining into a continuous stream over a 12-pulse span.

name: Kecak Cak Telu
desc: The interlocking 'cak telu' vocal pattern of the kecak monkey-chant chorus, transposing kotekan onto rhythmic 'cak' syllables split across three groups.

name: Kecak Cak Lima
desc: A five-part interlocking 'cak lima' division of the kecak chorus producing denser composite chatter, anchored by the slower pung/pur reciter line.

name: Gamelan Gong Gede
desc: The stately ceremonial 'great gong' orchestra of the Balinese courts, with broad gong cycles, kempur and kemong punctuation under slow trompong melody.

name: Baris Gilak
desc: The martial gilak ostinato accompanying the Balinese baris warrior dance, with gong and kempur framing a short repeating cycle of kajar and kendang accents.

name: Jaipongan
desc: Gugum Gumbira's drum-led Sundanese dance music: virtuosic kendang strokes derived from ketuk tilu and pencak silat punch syncopated accents off the beat over a gong cycle.

name: Kendang Penca
desc: The drum patterns accompanying Sundanese pencak silat, with sharp kendang strokes cueing and mirroring the martial-art movements of the fighters.

name: Ketuk Tilu
desc: The rural Sundanese social-dance form named for its 'three ketuk' kettle-gongs, a cyclic 4-beat measure punctuated by ketuk strikes with kendang off-beat propulsion.

name: Kulintang Binalig
desc: A fast, showy kagungudan-style Maguindanao rhythmic mode emphasising power and speed, with interlocking agung and dabakan driving the kulintang's complex improvisation.

name: Kulintang Sinulog
desc: The Maguindanao sinulog mode, rich in basic patterns and variations, with the agung interlocking against the dabakan in a steady cyclical ostinato.

name: Kulintang Tidto
desc: The tidto (tidtu) rhythmic mode, the most syncopated and least used for serenading, with sharply offset agung and dabakan accents under intricate kulintang play.

name: Kulintang Duyog
desc: The slow, dignified kamamatuan duyog (duyug) mode used to serenade, dominated by two closely related agung-and-dabakan patterns over an even kulintang pulse.

name: Kulintang Tagonggo
desc: The ritualistic tagonggo mode accompanying trance and dance ceremonies, with insistent interlocking agung and dabakan ostinatos rather than recreational kulintang melody.

name: Maranao Kapromayas
desc: A Maranao kulintang style from Lake Lanao, where agung and dabakan lock into a buoyant cyclical pattern beneath ornamented kulintang gong-row melody.

name: Piphat Na Thap Song Mai
desc: The medium-level (song chan) na thap drum cycle of the Thai piphat, with taphon and klong that strokes framed by the ching's open/closed timeline marking the cadence.

name: Piphat Na Thap Sam Mai
desc: The expansive third-level (sam chan) na thap cycle, broadly elaborated taphon and klong that patterns with the climactic accented ching 'chap' closing each cycle.

name: Ching Chan Diao
desc: The fundamental Thai ching timeline: an unaccented open 'ching' answered by an accented damped 'chap', the final chap (siang dok) carrying the strongest emphasis.

name: Klong That
desc: The paired barrel-drum klong that plays the primary beats of the Thai cycle, leaving gaps for the taphon to fill, together steering the piphat's tempo and dynamics.

name: Pinpeat Sampho
desc: The two-headed sampho drum leading the Cambodian pinpeat, controlling tempo and transitions while the chhing cymbals mark the metric framework of court and temple music.

name: Pinpeat Skor Thom
desc: The large paired skor thom barrel drums of the pinpeat sounding climactic signals and section cues, with gongs articulating cyclical time beneath the roneat and kong vong.

name: Hsaing Waing Pat Waing
desc: The tuned pat waing drum circle leading Myanmar's hsaing waing ensemble, producing melodic-rhythmic patterns unique among Southeast-Asian gong-chime orchestras.

name: Burmese Bonshay
desc: The bonshay metric pattern of Burmese classical song, articulated by the si (small bell) and wa (clapper) timeline that organises the hsaing waing's rhythm.

name: Vietnamese Cheo
desc: The northern Vietnamese folk-opera chèo, its trong (drum) and phách clapper marking the song's cyclic rhythm under sung narrative and dan nguyet lute.

name: Vietnamese Nha Nhac
desc: Vietnam's refined imperial court music of the Nguyen dynasty, with the trong chien drum and gongs framing a stately ceremonial cycle for ritual and temple performance.

name: Ca Tru Phach
desc: The intricate phách clapper rhythm of ca tru chamber song, the singer's wooden slats articulating an asymmetric cycle answered by the trong chau praise-drum.

name: Zapin
desc: An Arab-derived Johor dance in 4/4 built on interlocking marwas hand-drums playing alternating dum-tak figures with a gambus ostinato and the punctuating dok.

name: Joget
desc: A lively Portuguese-influenced Malay social dance in brisk 2/4 with a clear backbeat, propelled by rebana and violin for convivial partner dancing.

name: Inang
desc: A moderate, graceful 4/4 Malay courtly dance (also masri-related) with a light gendang pulse suited to refined, elegant movement.

name: Asli
desc: The slow, deeply ornamented Melayu asli song-form with a steady gendang cycle underpinning highly melismatic vocal lines and rubato openings.

name: Masri
desc: An Egyptian-flavoured (masri) Malay dance rhythm with a buoyant duple lilt carried by rebana and marwas hand-drums.

name: Ronggeng
desc: The convivial ronggeng/joget social-dance idiom in lively duple metre with a clear backbeat for couple dancing accompanied by violin, accordion and rebana.

name: Dondang Sayang
desc: The Malaccan pantun-exchange love song in moderate duple metre, its gentle gong, violin and rebana cycle leaving space for the singers' poetic repartee.

name: Talempong Pacik
desc: The hand-held Minangkabau gong-chimes of West Sumatra played by three musicians (anak on the downbeat, tengah between, peningkah off-beat) interlocking into a composite ostinato.

name: Gendang Melayu
desc: The double-headed gendang frame-drum patterns underpinning Malay dance, alternating deep 'pak' and high 'cak' strokes to drive joget, inang and zapin repertoire.

name: Gandang Tambua
desc: The thunderous interlocking gandang tambua double-headed drums of West Sumatra, multiple players locking dense composite rhythms for festive Minangkabau processions.

name: Lao Khaen Lam
desc: The lam singing tradition of Laos accompanied by the khaen mouth-organ, whose steady drone-and-drum cycle frames the sung poetry of the mor lam.
